newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Hoechst makes buyout move for Roussel.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Hoechst makes buyout move for Roussel.

text.p: German chemicals giant Hoechst AG, which holds 56.53 percent of Roussel Uclaf, announced on Wednesay an 18.1 billion franc ($3.5 billion) offer to buy out minority shareholders of the French pharmaceuticals group.

The move is a key step in Hoechst's creation of a simplified, legal identity for its Hoechst Marion Roussel (HMR) grouping formed last year with the $7.1 billion acquisition of U.S. Marion Merrell Dow.
HMR ranks fourth in the world pharmaceuticals market.

"This particular transaction is designed to maximise our opportunities in the pharmaceuticals area and come up with a Hoechst Marion Roussel operation which is globally integrated and which can therefore better face the competition," Hoechst finance director Klaus Schmieder told a news conference.
Industry analysts had been expecting Hoechst to bid for all Roussel as a step to a separate stock quotation for HMR.
But Schmieder said although Hoechst planned to issue its own shares on the New York stock exchange next year, any decision to float HMR would depend on the market valuation of its own stock.
"As long as we feel that the...stock price of Hoechst AG does not adequately reflect the value of the group, the listing of HMR becomes an issue and we will make a decision going forward," he said.
The simpler HMR structure following the Roussel buyout would however make it easier to launch an initial public offering for HMR if Hoechst decided to take that route, he said.

HMR had 1995 turnover of 44.7 billion francs and spent 6.5 billion in research and development. It employs 40,500 people and has 3.6 percent of the world pharmaceeutical market and a 3.7 percent share in the United States.
The buyout would boost its strength in Germany, France and the United States but would not raise its ranking behind Glaxo-Wellcome, Novartis and Merck.
The operation will be one of the biggest announced this year on the Paris bourse and continues the worldwide consolidation that is reshaping the pharmaceutical industry.

As part of the buyout negotiations Hoechst had to give the French government various undertakings, as the ERAP state-owned holding company owns 4.28 percent of Roussel, Schmieder said. ERAP has indicated it will tender its shares in the offer.

After the buyout, Roussel will maintain pre-clinical and clinical development in France, as well as run a major research centre at Romainville on the Paris suburbs, continue chemicals manufacture and create 700 new jobs for young people.
It will also maintain 220 million franc financing for various research programmes with public health authorities.

Commitments to maintaining jobs and investment by foreign companies taking over French firms has come under the spotlight recently following a rejection by the Privatisation Commission of a bid by South Korea's Daewoo Electronics for consumer electrincs firm Thomson Multimedia (TMM).
Hoechst is offering 1,530 francs per Roussel ordinary share and 1,330 francs per preference share, amounting to 18.1 billion francs, Hoechst said.
That represents a 12 percent premium on the average price of the common stock over the previous month and 19 percent over the average over the previous three months, Hoechst said.

The buyout is the second major transaction announced by Hoechst in two days. On Tuesday, it said it would merge its speciality chemicals business with Swiss group Clariant AG in a bid to overcome difficult conditions in the sector. ($1=5.218 French Franc)
